name: Russian Empire (Elizabeth)

areaKm2.note: world_1715 Tsardom of Muscovy polygon = 15,379,517 km2 on the sphere (incl. Siberia). Baltic provinces (1721) added after 1715.

population.note: Third revision (1762-63) ~23M for the empire as usually cited from Kabuzan; HYDE via OWID gives Russia (modern borders) 24.67M for 1760 plus Baltic provinces (Estonia 0.17M, Latvia part ~0.2M) and Left-bank Ukraine, which is the high end. Mid 23.5M.

urbanization.note: OWID urban share: Russia 2.0% (1750). Petersburg and Moscow ~150,000 each. Mid 3.5%.

activePersonnel.note: Duffy, Russia's Military Way to the West (1981) ch. 3: on paper ~330,000 c. 1756 including field regulars (~170,000), garrison troops (~75,000), the Ukrainian landmilitia and serving irregulars. Effectives were well below paper. Field army in Prussia 1759 ~60,000-70,000 (41,000 Russians at Kunersdorf, Battle of Kunersdorf article after Duffy 1996). audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess: recruits of the annual levy in depots, Cossack hosts (Don, Yaik) not yet called, and landmilitia not embodied.

supportPersonnel.note: Artillery and Shuvalov's Observation Corps gunners (~10,000), engineers, train, staff, and the navy (~15,000-20,000 for ~27 ships of the line and a large galley fleet).

mobilizationRatio.note: Paper strength ~330,000 on ~23M = 1.4%; levies of 1756-62 took ~230,000 recruits (Duffy ch. 3). Ceiling 3-4%. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Field infantry (46 musketeer and 4 grenadier regiments plus Guards) and garrison battalions, at effective rather than paper strength (Duffy ch. 3). audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5 (era-typical) to 0.75 (among the era best). Evidence: flintlock-bayonet, era-typical; good grenadiers

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5-0.75. Evidence: lifetime-service conscripts, slow to manoeuvre, notoriously steady in defence (Zorndorf, Kunersdorf)

count.note: Educated guess: light infantry (jager) battalions only formed by Rumyantsev in 1761; grenadier detachments used as light troops.

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: new units

count.note: Cuirassier regiments (6) and horse grenadiers (Duffy ch. 3). audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: poor horses

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: weak heavy cavalry

count.note: Dragoon regiments (~20,000), hussar regiments (~6,000) and Cossacks and Kalmyks serving with the field army (~15,000-20,000) (Duffy ch. 3). Dragoons counted as light cavalry. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: Cossacks excellent at raiding (Berlin raid Oct 1760)

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.5. Evidence: mixed regulars and irregulars

count.note: The allied Russo-Austrian army at Kunersdorf had 248 guns (Battle of Kunersdorf article, Duffy 1996 p. 235); the Russian field army carried a very large artillery park incl. Shuvalov unicorns. Total field pieces estimated 350-800.

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.75. Evidence: Shuvalov secret howitzers and unicorns, heavy batteries; Russian artillery considered among the most numerous of the war

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.75. Evidence: professional artillery corps

count.note: Glete, Navies and Nations (1993): Russian Baltic fleet c. 1760 ~25-30 ships of the line, many in poor condition; blockade of Kolberg 1760-61. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: short-lived Baltic-built ships

training.note: Rubric row: training 0.25-0.5. Evidence: little sea time

count.note: Educated guess: frigates, prams and the Baltic galley fleet (~100 galleys in the archipelago flotilla).

quality.note: Rubric row: quality 0.5. Evidence: galleys for skerries

commandQuality.note: Rubric row: commandQuality 0.5. Evidence: Saltykov won Kunersdorf (1759) but cautious; the Conference in Petersburg micromanaged; Rumyantsev rising

cohesion.note: Rubric row: cohesion 0.75. Evidence: lifetime service, regiment as home; Russian infantry held at Zorndorf and Kunersdorf

morale.note: Rubric row: morale 0.75. Evidence: Gross-Jagersdorf (1757), Kunersdorf (1759), occupation of East Prussia and the Berlin raid (1760)

weapons.note: Anchor: 5.8 near 6 (1805). Evidence: flintlock-bayonet line infantry and Shuvalov unicorn howitzers

ships.note: Anchor: 5.6. Evidence: Baltic-built 66-gun ships, weaker than British or French

fortification.note: Anchor: 5.7. Evidence: Vauban-type fortresses at Riga, Kyiv, Petersburg

logistics.note: Anchor: 5.3. Evidence: magazines on the Vistula from 1758; operations in Prussia hampered by supply (Duffy ch. 4)

communications.note: Anchor: 5.3. Evidence: courier post; Petersburg to the army in Brandenburg ~2 weeks

isr.note: Anchor: ISR uses the same years as the anchor table (1600 -> 5, 1805 -> 6). Evidence: cavalry screens, spies and merchant reports only; no aerial or signal intelligence

air.note: No aircraft or military balloons before 1783/1794.

gdpPerCapita.note: Analogue: Poland 1760 = 1,019 (Maddison Project 2023, https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true); Russia taken at the Polish level. No Maddison Project series exists for Russia before 1820 (checked MPD 2020 and MPD 2023 via OWID); analogue = Poland (MPD 2023).

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high), 2011 int$.

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess: army and navy took over half of a state revenue of ~15M rubles; war year 1760.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess: Urals iron (Russia the largest pig-iron producer in Europe by 1760s), textiles; overwhelmingly agrarian.

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess: black-earth surplus growing; low northern yields.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.009-0.011 (mid 0.0095): in a pre-transition age structure (Wrigley and Schofield type, life expectancy ~30-35) males reaching 18 each year are about 0.9-1.1% of total population. Males only.

roadKm.note: Educated guess: post roads Petersburg-Moscow-Riga-Kyiv; most unpaved.

majorPorts.note: Kronstadt, Petersburg, Reval, Riga, Pernau, Arkhangelsk, plus occupied Konigsberg/Pillau.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess: Russian exports moved mostly on British and Dutch ships.

supplyRangeKm.note: van Creveld, Supplying War (isbn:0-521-54657-5) ch. 1: 17th-18th c. armies tied to magazines and bread ovens, operating ~5 marches (~100-150 km) beyond the nearest magazine or navigable river; requisition extends it in rich country. Russian operations in Brandenburg depended on Vistula magazines and repeatedly stalled. audit 2026-10-30: grade C -> D: cited by ISBN only, with no fetched copy of the book (SOURCES.md grading rule).

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess: peasant horses and oxen for ~23M people.

homeDefense.note: 1.3 row: deep strategic depth and harsh winter; not tested on Russian soil in this war.

notes: Snapshot = 1760, Seven Years War (Russian occupation of East Prussia, raid on Berlin in October). Population: Russian Empire incl. Baltic provinces and Left-bank Ukraine. Personnel convention: field and garrison regulars and irregulars serving with the field army are active; landmilitia not embodied, depot recruits and uncalled Cossack hosts are trainedReserves. Duffy's paper strengths (book, not fetched; cited from Russia's Military Way to the West, ch. 3) are the anchor; effectives were well below. GDP per head is a regional analogy (no Maddison series for Russia before 1820).
